I recall how differently Americans responded during the Viet Nam war. Protesters took to the streets, often in great numbers. Protests and strikes shut down roads, businesses, government offices. Protest activity was widespread and effective. It was a very large impetus for ending that war.

And now?  Now, when we're far further down the road to fascism than could be credibly imagined in the Sixties?

And there is no way many members of my family and I share what Trump (a newcomer) or Vance (another newcomer) believe. That is the exact opposite of what our families stood for. 

The inscription on the Statue of Liberty, by Emma Lazarus, states in part, "Give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free." That means everyone, not some country-club membership structure. That is what our families stood for.

If you want to join a country club to avoid brown or black people, go ahead, but a country club is not America. What Emma Lazarus said reflects exactly what generations of my family, both believed and fought for: FREEDOM! 

Freedom is and always should be America...for everyone. Reagan may not have been one of my favorite presidents, but his "shining city on the hill " speech has its merits. And to paraphrase a little bit from that speech, Nothing is less free than pure communism (and fascism). Both seek to control- they are the very opposite of freedom.

On the revenue side, it’s time to admit that our century-old experiment with the income tax has been a failure. The tax code – countless thousands of pages defining personal and business income and allowable expenses – is a perpetual game of Whack-A-Mole, providing full employment for accountants, lawyers and lobbyists. 

And the bottom line: Since World War II, federal revenue has been mostly stuck between 16% – 19% of GDP, even as the top marginal tax rate has bounced between 28% and 91%.

The alternative? Replace the income tax with the Land Value Tax. Land ownership is the primary source of unearned, unproductive inequality. If you got rich inventing that Better Mousetrap, then you earned it, keep your money. But the oceanfront view that makes your plot of land valuable – you didn’t build that! Taxing land simplifies not only the calculation of taxes owed but also enforcement - you can try to hide income but you can’t hide land.

Taxing land instead of income would be both good politics and good economics, progressive and pro-growth. The wealthy owners of high-priced land would provide a disproportionate share of the revenue (the top 1 percent own 40 percent of all land value), but the marginal tax on income would be ZERO – a win-win for both “liberals” and “conservatives”.

comments.name: Truth be told …

Why does the Roberts Court consider “electioneering communications”  more fundamental to a “fair voice and representation” in government than the exercise of our free speech rights when we cast our ballots?

In Citizens United, the Court reasoned,

“…the government may commit a constitutional wrong when by law it identifies certain preferred speakers. By taking the right to speak from some and giving it to others, the government deprives the disadvantaged person or class of the right to use speech to strive to establish worth, standing, and respect for the speaker’s voice. The government may not by these means deprive the public of the right and privilege to determine for itself what speech and speakers are worthy of consideration. The First Amendment protects speech and speaker, and the ideas that flow from each.”

When state government representatives gerrymander they violate the Free Speech Clause, by identifying “certain preferred speakers,” i.e., voters, in order to predetermine for the public the worth of certain classes of voters in their states, on the basis of political-party affiliation, etc. In so doing, they deprive the “disadvantaged person[s] or class of the right to use speech[,i.e., their votes,] to strive to establish worth, standing, and respect for [their] voice” as solemnized in their ballots.

When we vote, we speak; we express in writing whom we want to represent us and whom we do not want to represent us, based on shared political values.

... the group frankly views the party it occupies as a host for an ideological movement rather than as a partner. The Democratic Party does not have an heir apparent, and that is a good thing. A party that puts “Democratic” in its name should let voters choose its next leader.
There is a difference between having prominent contenders and having someone whose nomination is treated as a foregone conclusion, like in the cases of Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris. Nobody owns the next nomination. The last time the Democrats were in that position we got Barack Obama, a young, charismatic, intelligent, moderate.
Coronations fail. Competition gives voters a chance to examine the real person, especially in light of today’s 24-hour news cycles and social media. Little gets by.
The absence of an heir apparent also creates space for new leadership. Governors, senators, and less familiar figures can make their cases alongside established names. Experience deserves consideration, but seniority should not come with a guarantee of nomination. Neither should fundraising connections, television exposure, or the blessing of party insiders be the deciding factors.
Democrats also need a serious debate about why voters support them, and a realistic candidate will understand the vast majority of Americans are not interested in what the DSA is selling. If they fail to recognize that then they will once again squander an opportunity to regain control of our democracy.

Indeed, several of these men had never even laid a hand on Jane Doe. The tragedy in Nepal should not become another argument between people who believe climate change is real and people who don't. The more interesting question is what actually caused this mountain to fail.

That is also why the headline, “The Glaciers Are Collapsing,” troubles me. The event described in the article involved a massive failure of rock and glacier ice, not simply a glacier melting or collapsing. Evidence points to instability in the underlying bedrock. Warming and thawing permafrost may have contributed, and that possibility deserves serious investigation. But “may have contributed” and “caused” are not interchangeable.

That doesn't weaken the case for monitoring. It strengthens it. Mountain communities face landslides, rockfalls, debris flows and glacier hazards for many reasons. If satellite observations can detect dangerous acceleration and provide useful warning, we should use them regardless of the ultimate attribution.

The people of Nepal deserve something better than another climate argument. They deserve an accurate diagnosis of what happened and a warning system based on what the evidence actually tells us.

A headline should reflect that evidence too.

As informative as this conversation was, I'm amazed that there was not more of a discussion about the massive amounts of debt that are financing the A.I. boom.  If there is a crash, it's going to be as a result of all the debt and an inability to debt service it.

I posted a comment earlier about the freefall of CoreWeave, but there is another debt story that is as (or more) concerning because it is a legacy tech company that has made a huge bet on A.I.  That company is Oracle.

Oracle's stock is down almost 50% since Sept 2025. But it gets worse. S&P Global Ratings downgraded Oracle's long-term issuer credit rating to BBB- from BBB in July, and cut its short-term rating, according to the agency's report. 

That leaves Oracle just one notch above junk status.  Sit with that one for a moment.

And there's more.

S&P also flagged Oracle's exposure to OpenAI, which makes up approximately half of Oracle's $638 billion order backlog. That means if OpenAI ever struggles to pay its bills, Oracle could get stuck holding data center leases it can't easily exit. 

As if that wasn't bad enough, Oracle's total liabilities have increased from $147.4 billion to $218.7 billion in just 12 months.

Of course, Oracle thinks its A.I. bet will pay off. But there are plenty of warning signs that it might not.  We will all pay the price if the sages at Oracle are wrong.

That its developers and owners would release such untested models demonstrates its weaknesses as well as that we can't trust its developers.

. Corporations are fanatical about laying off people to cut costs and boost their stock prices.  Sadly, they're still following the "Jack Welch" slash and burn business model*.  Corporations are rushing to deploy A.I. even though it doesn't work and customers are frustrated.  Sooner or later corporations will wake up to the discontent they've created and have to cut back on A.I.

The beach house for instance brings to mind elements of Chinatown and the long goodbye and I think they took that into the design of the film. And that gorgeous dissolve from Nathan’s profile to his car driving down a country road to Amanda Seyfried’s house.

comments.name: Lindsey
comments.body: I found myself thinking “gosh maybe she is just that naive” which was the effect of brilliant filmmaking. The Who’s on first scene set me back to reality. Lizzy Blood Drop is a fantastic case study of utter manipulation in an effort to fulfill a childhood dream.

comments.name: Dawid
comments.body:
This felt like a film that may come to be studied by, or at least shown to, undergraduate students across various subject matters: philosophy, psychology, ethics, sociology, business, law… I thought it was a highly compelling close-up (sometimes very literally) of at least 3 master manipulators taking a story that has high public interest value and trying to shape it in whatever ways they could towards their own end goals. 

It is at times hard to reconcile how someone who presents herself as naively as Ms. Holmes attempts to do might have ever been a titan of industry. Mr. Evans appears to out himself as a rare parasite that preys on other parasites. Mr. Fielder made an incredibly unique film in a style that he’s all but perfected by now.

comments.name: Reveala99
comments.body: I saw this movie without knowing anything about Fielder or even having seen any of his earlier work. In fact, I was surprised how many times the audience in the theater with me, laughed long and loudly during the early exchanges. They clearly thought they were seeing “a bit” and I felt I was seeing two people holding their ground during points they were making. One thing about cameras is that when they are on you so consistently as they appear to be in this movie, at some point you see a break. When Evans and Holmes had an off camera discussion where their mics were still hot he told her impatiently that she has to stand up for herself. I thought that line and exchange was very telling. My takeaway from this is that Holmes may be on the spectrum and genuinely doesn’t see things the way others do, as in the Abbot &  Costello bit. But maybe I’m just de facto pro women and feel that she’s a brilliant person with emotional/intellectual challenges who’s been manipulated by someone more conventionally intellectual (Evans).

comments.name: J Knapp
comments.body:
I think Fielder is a genius, and this movie is more evidence of such. I worried going into it that he couldn’t top The Rehearsal, and that I had hyped the film in my head in such a way that could only produce some level of letdown, but wow was I wrong! Fielder blends elements of all his past acts into a magnum opus, and it’s a wonder to behold.

When not clawing my face off during Billy scenes, I was dying laughing. Like soda through the nose almost drowning laughing at the out-of-nowhere hilarity… (The dad saying he worked for Enron, Amanda Siegfried vs. Billy vs. Kirk, the random romance element and “flirting”, etc). 

But what Fielder really masters here is a rumination on truth. I think some viewers missed the point that there’s no need to litigate what happened in the past directly on screen—he is serving these people up to you and letting you see them UP CLOSE. He is allowing us to decide what we believe and don’t, as in the scene where Fielder and Seyfried are trying to determine if Holmes knew about the payment Billy insisted on before shooting. It felt like a nod to Larry David’s bit in Curb where he stares people down to determine if they’re being truthful the way the camera operates to focus closely on Holmes’ unblinking eyes.

Do not approach this as a doc about Holmes or Theranos. Those already exist. This is a brilliant meta exploration about truth in its various forms and who’s telling it (if anyone). To quote Amanda, “It’s just TV.” And WOW does it entertain!

comments.name: Sara I
comments.body:
There are so many things to say about this fascinating film.
To me, one of the most astonishing things about it, is how much it forces us the viewers to take heed of ourselves. In every instance of thinking about one thread or another in the film, I arrive ultimately at the idea that my perceptions and presumptions have been well challenged if not obliterated utterly. What an exciting dynamic for a film to create--this psychological maze which forces us to also turn a lens on ourselves. Watching it is so much more than a viewing experience.

comments.body: I saw the film last night and found it compelling; the three hours flew by. Unlike any other documentary I have seen. Definitely not flattering to Holmes or her monstrous husband. And as always with Fielder, it also manages to be funnier than almost anything else out there.

Fights over a spoon are much bloodier than a fight over cash.

Ive seen three or four instances where parents leave the cottage to the kids jointly, “to keep it the family.”  It always ends badly; sometimes even breaking up the family.  When I’m gone, we have a provision that has a third party value the property in the event a family member wants to buy it from siblings.  Otherwise it will be sold on the open market.

It's a good reminder that estate planning is as much about communication as it is about financial planning.

comments.name: Jaganathan
comments.body:
Theranos exposed a deep vulnerability in modern medicine, but its true lesson extends beyond Silicon Valley’s hubris. The real danger today is our cultural obsession with the isolated diagnostic baseline.
Whether it is a 50-analyte panel or direct-to-consumer genetic sequencing, a laboratory test taken out of context is not information—it is noise. Human biology does not exist as a static list of numbers. A genetic variant or an elevated enzyme means nothing until filtered through a thinking clinician who evaluates the living patient: the detailed clinical history, physical examination, and dynamic interplay of physiology over time.
When direct-to-consumer genomics promises to predict disease without clinical correlation, it fails for the exact same reason Theranos failed: it substitutes quantitative pan-testing for clinical context. A high pre-test probability transforms a test into a diagnostic key; a zero pre-test probability transforms the same test into an engine of false positives, unnecessary anxiety, and cascade interventions.
Neither AI nor automation can replace the essential diagnostic act: a human mind integrating history, bedside observation, and critical reasoning to formulate a hypothesis before a single drop of blood is drawn. Evaluate before you test. Without clinical context, any technology remains fundamentally blind.
The prose of this commentary was structured with AI assistance, but the clinical argument and core thesis belong entirely to the author.

I read through most of the comments and haven't yet seen anyone mention the relationship between AI and debt rates. Over the past year, hyperscalers and neocloud providers have shifted their financing of new data centers to debt. There's only so much demand for debt, and when both the Treasury and AI companies are competing for the same investors it's natural that rates will rise. It sounds crazy, but there's enough debt financing of AI to move the needle on rates.

When the AI bubble pops I expect that high quality bonds are going to do just fine as rates drop. Of course equities are headed down too, since AI-related equities have been masking a downturn in the rest of the market. There will be some really good buying opportunities in a few months.

Bulimics and anorexics have long tried medicating themselves - EG laxatives, diuretics, and amphetamines - to eliminate the urges to eat (ie hunger) and lose body weight.  GLPs, unlike those medications, actually do work to reduce the drive to eat and are far more effective causing weight loss. Overlooked here are the cardinal symptoms of body image distortion and dysmorphia that characterize eating disorders, and prevent users from accepting that they are emaciated, hence endangering them.

comments.name: JV
comments.body:
Anorexia is devastating to the body and soul. I had anorexia when I was younger. Badly. This is very scary to me. I never went back to any type of diet- but I worked harder on getting better than I had for anything. It took a summer of an iop and lots of individual therapy. I was lucky because my parents were absolutely alarmed and they could afford to pay for my treatment. Not everyone is so lucky. 

I have no answer here except it is very true it’s hard to identify for doctors. What makes it harder is people often want to keep the disorder. I did for a while until I realized it was controlling me. I had one doctor- a new ob/gyn who is a woman that asked me straight up. I lied. She asked me to come back to be weighed in two weeks. I’m embarrassed to say I wore lots of layers and put rolls of quarters in my pockets. We are hard to spot when protecting the disease.

That’s how scared I was to be found out. But she was amazing and unflinchingly honest with me. My mom started seeing her too and she told the doctor she saved my life. She did- I credit her with my beginning to acknowledge I had a very real problem. Ask.

Anorexia kills- it has the highest rate of mortality out of the dsm. Please get help if you’re concerned about disordered eating- it’s a slippery slope. One thing treatment did was make me see how society treats women. So I developed confidence in myself and my body and feel like I got to skip years of self doubt I saw my friends go through. It’s truly freeing!

I think as you get older it makes less sense to be too thin. But despite my logical brain, my emotional sense sees thinness as a competition with myself and the idea of youthfulness or the stupidity of my youth where thinness was equated with beauty. My husband loves me and I love him, but I often see myself as too fat or okay like the day is a funhouse mirror. The drug seems like a way to step out of my body and never give it a thought. So, doctors should at least see the person asking for the drug! Because our youth continue to live in our minds!

comments.body:
I’m going to both agree and disagree. First the agreement. We have seen in our family the adverse and unpredictable impact of dementia on behaviors. Clearly at some point dementia reaches the level of incompetence, often realized later, not sooner. Discussions about risks in the home and (e.g.) the car have to be had sooner, not later. Those risks are to the self and to others.
The statistics you see about “gun deaths” includes suicides, which comprise over half (62%) per CDC with homicides committed against others, 35% and Law Enforcement the balance. I don’t know where the ICE murders fit. Giffords, which is a biased entity, puts the Gun Homicide rate at 40% and suicides at 56%. In any case gun homicides as a proportion of gun deaths is declining. Suicide is up, and I suspect age and economic factors are drivers.
Our culture is influenced by religio-philosophical beliefs embedded in Judeo-Christian tenets, counting suicide as murder. There are many other cultures that see it as acceptable in certain circumstances or at least tolerated. I think we ought to consider that. I believe suicide is an option everyone has. Your belief system is yours and should not be imposed on the potentially suicidal person might be talking about. Saving oneself from the final throes of terminal illness, having myself seen both cancers and dementia, ought to be a right retained at the personal level.

comments.name: Eric S.
comments.body: Should a senior have the right to end their own life, when declining health and related problems become unmanageable for them? Should we make every effort to prevent them from taking the initiative to end their life? I see that as a different kind of problem than when a senior, obviously out-of-touch or delusional, threatens the lives of others, because of impaired judgement. The procedural barriers that are in place in states that have provision for assisted suicide may seem like an unnecessary hassle for some. While we have every reason to prevent suicide on impulse, with no compelling reason, there are situations where intervention may simply add to the individual's problems, at least from their perspective.

comments.name: Peg
comments.body:
A huge advantage of manufactured homes (it seems taboo to use the name mobile home anymore due to stigma) is that when you need repairs or a new heater or water heater or roof, etc., you really can just hire a handyman or do-it-yourself and save thousands.  

If you only want a 12-20 gallon water heater for the whole house (maybe a single person) you can do that as well, or if you want to use a portable heat pump as your main heating and cooling costing hundreds instead of thousands, you can do that too.  

Trades influenced building codes, often require massive whole house systems costing thousands for regular homes, but are often not needed by older folks or in milder climates.

Building codes need to change so more can afford to ditch the gas for plug in heatpumps.

These codes often make it far too expensive to switch from gas to electric for environmental reasons as you often need to hire a plumber and an electrician, when in reality, small 120 volt plug-in portable heat pumps and water tanks exist. 

However, none of this large expense is required if you live in a manufactured home since the same building codes to not apply to the interior.  Being "mobile" even though most are not very mobile and are affixed to the land which you may also own, means they are classified more like an RV even though these days they can be hard to distinguish from a regular house and are well insulated with shingle roofs etc.

There is lower insurance and property tax as, well.

comments.name: riverrunner
comments.body: Having worked as a carpenter building  stick-built housing 50 years ago, and  now  looking at quality pre-fab housing being built currently (I am downsizing),  I believe quality pre-fab housing could set off a much-needed burst of creativity and  innovation in home-building in the U.S.   Architectural advances that reduce energy costs and improve structural integrity in extreme weather,  the precision of factory-built construction, installing plumbing and electrical distribution during  structure construction, utilization of advances in structural materials,   including  dramatic improvements in materials that increase a structure's insulating ability, as well as remain intact in extreme weather that destroys stick-built homes in extreme weather - together  could set off a creative explosion in homebuilding that is sorely needed.   Unfortunately,  these changes are being held up by a failure to update building codes that were designed for stick-built homes, the NIMBY fear of change and innovation,  and in many cases, arbitrary restrictions set by HOAs, that are not part of  code regulation.   For now,  innovators who have a record of success, who have GCs who are willing, and competent at,  onsite preparation, and conversations with homeowners who have been in the company's homes for a year or more, if possible, are all good ideas.   We need this revolution in home-building.   Try to avoid the errors that are inevitable in innovation.

comments.name: Asta
comments.body:
I've owned a prefab in my home town that was about 15 years old when I bought it and have had it for almost 20. It's ok, but you do have to watch for settling. The build is comparable to other houses in the area of the time and era - not great, poor insulation. So it really does depend on your area whether prefab is done well or not.

In construction, you can save time or you can save money, but it's highly unlikely to save both. Last month, I considered a prefab for a garage as I plan to move back full time.The area (mid-Atlantic) has turned into a resort community, so the prefab guys are pushing hard "everything included." I got one estimate from a stick built company and they were 1/2 the price of a prefab company for the same thing. The timing for both were comparable. I've done several gut renos as my own GC, so I'm getting blueprints and will piece it out to save money and get a better quality build to my needs, but it won't save time. 

For the OP, get several bids from both stick built and prefab companies. Many stick built companies have "models" that you can choose from and customize as needed. Be sure to ask about your involvement and timing to compare. Many stick built guys also have someone to do the blueprints cost effectively, and your house will be more custom to you. And remember, you can tour a stick built house any time and make changes, prefab you're not going in the factory all the time. Good luck!

comments.name: MerinMaberly
comments.body: We chose a factory-built home for many reasons, including the quality of the product and design variations within each floorplan. Our ICF lower level walk out was formed and poured onsite in mid July of 2024, our upper story prefab was delivered and dropped in mid August. We moved in November 11, 2024. Granted, we had odds and ends yet to do, like tiling the downstairs bath, replacing the construction stairs, installing balcony railings, but our upper level kitchen and bathroom counters were delivered installed; the toilets only required bolting on. In contrast, neighbors were still plodding away at their home 10-months later. The great thing is needing fewer onsite trades people to complete the project as scheduling is usually an issue. Plug and play is the way to go.

comments.name: martello
comments.body: in the 1970s my father had a "mobile home" sales business so we wound up living in two. As an adult, over the years I have bought and lived for years in three "mobile homes" aka "double wides"and all three were some of the best homes I've ever lived in. None had any difficulties from their transportation, and think about it: something built to withstand being driven over a highway at 55 miles per hour has to be built pretty robustly. They also have been cheapest to heat of all the homes I've owned, especially the one built in Nebraska to Nebraska winter standards. The only problem I ever had was when I went to sell the one that was in a very nice neighborhood of otherwise only stick-built homes, and the appraiser and real estate agent had a heck of a time trying to find value comps. Each of my homes appreciated in value rather than depreciated, as is the common perception. Manufactured homes are an excellent alternative for people who don't have a ton of money to invest but want a nice home, but the caveat is it should be on its own land rather than in a rental park.

comments.body: Interesting article that states plenty of facts relevant to its readers but what the Journal misses here is the longer, broader view to contemplate.  Our economic growth has in significant part been fueled for centuries by financiers inventing new ways to use our own societal wealth to raise the overall standard of living. Those at the frontiers of this expansion trod a bumpy road. Pick any entrepreneur, titan of industry, lord of finance, etc… and you’ll find setbacks, including those that took longer than expected to overcome. It’s good to talk about the bumps  but it’s equally important to understand that they come with the territory. It’s widely acknowledged that we are entering another industrial revolution, probably the most capital intensive one yet. New financial tools will, as always in such leaps forward, contribute to a faster, stronger, and more beneficial result for us and our future generations. As such, private debt and funding of data centers is something we should all wish the best for while understanding nobody can get such things done in a straight line. comments.name: Cate
comments.body:
There is a serious need for societies around the world to finally recognize and begin to seriously investigate male values.

This week in particular has been full of devastating news about some men's inability to find a set of beliefs within themselves and our society (in which they have so much influence),
that isn't about violence: at least three wars are currently in progress, one tragic elementary school shooting, revelations of a fraternity house alleged "male gang rape" of a young woman a few years back, attitudes on the part of male leadership in which there is blatant hostility toward those with whom they disagree on various topics. 

There is a daily barrage of stories laced with the cruelty or neglect or damage being inflicted upon whole populations of people across the globe.

What is the matter with men? Where are the expectations we once had not too long ago of male rationality, male leadership, male example of high moral and behavioral standards visible on a daily basis as they moved through society with strong compassion, with a sense of moral direction?

In the 80 years of my life I have watched within the past fifty years or so a rapid and alarming sense of decay of our human spirit--a loss that has become so commonplace as to shed a pall of sorrow over our sense of decency as human beings.

Men need to get back to showing themselves to be interested primarily in compassion in their daily lives. Otherwise, it's all over for all of us--we're not worth saving.

comments.name: Kalidan
comments.body:
The extent to which the commentary from readers suggests sugar consumption is bad leaves me rather discouraged.  As if the article is litigating the virtues of processed sugar, and not about nature-made (El Nino) catastrophe worsened likely by human devotion to fossil fuel that is hurting the poorest of the poor.  

Any other crop in its place, regardless of its connection to processed carbs, would likely have had triggered similar tragedy.  No rain is bad news for any crop; it leaves a longish chain reaction of worse events including farmer suicides.  This is what the article is really about.

It is outrageous that people think reducing sugar consumption is anything but a tertiary issue.  India is vulnerable in serious ways; glacial fed perennial rivers are subject to retreating glaciers (and inordinate filth and industrial waste dumped), and the southern rivers are iffy.  What the nation may benefit from is connected waterways, but of course, that only results in a political money and power grab in India at the expense of helpless people.

Just so readers know, the amount of ethanol in petrol in India is close to 30%, because ethanol production is controlled by the progeny of a big shot politician.  It is, and will, wreak havoc on the millions of small gas fed machines Indians use (scooters, motorcycles, pumps, farm equipment). 

Conflating drought with sugar consumption is really pretty cruel, and doing so with the smug self-satisfaction displayed here is disgusting.

I am an immigrant. My family fled Czechoslovakia in 1967. While we are not Jewish, my father fell in love with the USA when American soldiers liberated Prague at the end of WWll. Our escape was from totalitarianism. 

What you write makes perfect sense to me. 

Since I was very young when we arrived in the States, I have spent a majority of my life as a US citizen. Still, the first time I visited Prague in March of 1989, and on every subsequent trip, I felt so deeply grounded, it surprised me. Hearing my native language, seeing the beauty of the country, tasting and smelling food that was only served in my home, being surrounded by people who looked like me also filled me with an incredible sense of belonging. I say this because despite the almost 60 years I have called the US my home, Czechia will always be my homeland.

comments.name: Sidi
comments.body:
I have to correct a mistaken belief that you wrote about Austrians confronting their murderous past starting in 1980, long after Germany.   
In 1991 our Chancellor addressed parliament for the first time in to start and confront history and the huge lie that was embraced for generations that Austria was Hitler’s victim.  Austrians were passionate about welcoming Hitler in March 1938, except for those running for their lives.  
Even today we have people who are unable to face their past history generation after generation and their are schools which continue with an extremely superficial education of the Holocaust.  
We don’t read books of horror like Cold Crematorium.   We read Anne Frank, year after year.  I have tried to have a government mandatory book list on the subject to no effect.  We have students who get their information from internet and wouldn’t read those books anyway.
Hence, we have students who have “heard” the name Hitler but know nothing else.

I have lived here 36 years so I have much experience on all aspects of history, past and present.

comments.name: ALEX
comments.body:
Liebe Grüße aus Österreich!

Your family’s story reminds us how deeply identity is tied to the place we call home.

We should remember that most Austrians and Germans didn't hate Jews. Some helped their Jewish neighbors, risking arrest, imprisonment, or even their lives. Others remained silent out of fear, while many supported the regime. While the full extent of the atrocities in concentration and extermination camps was not known, persecution and deportations were visible. These distinctions matter without diminishing historical responsibility.

But history must also guide us today.
America is heading down a dark and dangerous path, one that echoes troubling chapters of our history.
In the US, ICE raids, deportations, and hostility toward immigrants and minorities raise serious concerns about dignity and belonging. Meanwhile, Palestinian families face displacement, destruction, and immense suffering.

These situations are not historically identical, but they remind us how dangerous dehumanization can become.

We can honor Jewish history, oppose antisemitism, criticize the Israeli government’s actions, and defend the rights of Palestinians and immigrants alike.

Perhaps gemütlich means ensuring that everyone can feel safe, respected, and at home.

“Never Again” must mean everyone, no exception, even not your government.

Ihr müsst dafür aber wirklich kämpfen.
Servus und alles Gute bei den Midterms!

Her mother was a  Catholic primarily of Slovenian ancestry and her father was a Muslim from Sarejevo, which gives some indication of the ethnic and cultural complexity that existed in Austria prior and during world war II. comments.name: Istvaniffy
comments.body:
Pope Leo was raised in essentially a very working class white community of Dolton Illinois before its dramatic racial transformation that took place.  The dramatic racial transformation of Dolton took place primarily between 1980 and 2000, with the most rapid changes occurring during the 1980s and early 1990s. The accompanying economic decline developed over roughly the same period, as manufacturing jobs disappeared from the south suburbs of Chicago.

But the toxic exposure of industrial pollution on the Pope when an nfant and a child is obvious. Children breathe faster and take in more air relative to their body size than adults. Industrial pollutants like and nitrogen dioxide damage developing airways, reduce lung function, and increase the risk of childhood asthma, bronchitis, and respiratory infections.

Dolton is in southern Cook County, an area with a substantial history of steelmaking, manufacturing, freight transportation, and industrial emissions.

The difference in life expectancy between Dolton and Chicago’s North Shore suburbs is substantial—roughly 8 to 15 years, depending on which North Shore community you compare it with. The available data show a striking geographic disparity in health and longevity across the Chicago metropolitan area. 

The Pope was put at greater cancer risk simply based on where he grew up and both of Pope Leo XIV’s parents had cancer during their lifetimes. This hasn’t been discussed much in the media.

For heaven's sake, nobody knows what the future holds.  A cancer diagnosis is never a good thing, but the fact that an operation took place that now has the pope returning to his normal routine is a good sign that Leo still maintains a pretty strong constitution, and the prognosis is uncertain but hopeful.

I realize that journalists love feeding the public stories about "what if" this or "what if" that, and it's never entirely surprising to speak about one's life and legacy, certainly once one reaches the age of 70.  But there is every reason to believe that Leo could have a good decade or more still left in him, and let's hope he does.  It would appear that the immediate prognosis for Leo is good.  I don't see the current situation meriting "pressing questions about life and legacy."  I don't think we're anywhere near that stage yet.  Let's hope not, anyway.

I am opening boxes and putting away my things in my new home having just left a 3 year marriage at the age of 76. My soon to be ex-wife has serious anger issues that I felt would eventually kill me if I didn't leave. She had a hair trigger temper and at times vebrally, emotionally and yes, physically abused me.  Fights went on for days and she would say things that I call "hitting below the belt" that one cannot take back. 

I never struck her and tried to be a peacmaker. We attended counseling and she herself say a therapist but to no avail. She was abused a child by her father and step father while my parents were happily married for 58 years and never fought in a confrontational matter. Who knows what the casue was of all this, but true to form she blamed me for her anger towards me. 

It became what is called a "cycle of abuse" that never stopped and no matter what good times we had, her anger outweighed it all.

It is not easy to break free, but as I put my feet up and watch a good game today I realize that sometimes you have to leave angry people no matter how much effort they may make.

comments.name: JRC
comments.body: When I turned 70 I decided to make the attempt to rid myself of anger and to develop methods to deal with anger that might be expressed towards me from someone else. I found out it is very difficult to change behavior patterns. Yet, anger saps mental, emotional and physical energy and usually does not lead to a satisfactory resolution of the underlying problem. What I’ve tried to do is replace an angry reaction with other less destructive responses. Disappointment, sadness, even frustration are much better outlets for reacting to situations that previously resulted in an eruption of anger. Of course, talking out the problem and coming up with viable solutions is the best course of action but not always feasible. If anger is directed at me I try to remove myself from the situation until the other individual is calm enough to have a rational conversation. This has been a slow process but my own anger has been greatly reduced. Patience with oneself is key.

comments.name: Mortimer MacGuffin

'Serenity Now', say it with me, 'Serenity Now'. Whenever you feel an anger attack coming on say those two words out loud. Whenever your frustration level rises into the danger zone, voicing 'Serenity Now' will quell the savage beast, but ya gotta mean it. Throwing a bag of groceries at your husband seems an endpoint, when frustration rises to anger, but groceries are a fairly innocuous thing to throw at someone, not to mention awkward to throw. My 1st thought was, what was in the bag of groceries? If it was bread then it would be like throwing a pillow. If it was frozen steaks then it could be considered a weapon. If I was to throw a bag of groceries at someone, I would first consider how much the groceries cost and are any of the groceries at risk of being damaged which costs money or if there was milk in the bag, would it make a mess that needs cleaning up. After assessing the pros and cons then I would decide if the bag of groceries was worth making a statement. Just sayin.

PS: I can't remember the last time I was angry but I do remember the last time someone was angry at me.

So once Catharina lost ready access to her father's accumulated materials and other paraphernalia such as easels, canvas, a room with proper lighting and much more—she was suddenly bereft of all but her truly wonderful talent? There are myriad real undescribed species out there in the rainforest and the deep ocean, that are going to go extinct without ever being discovered because researchers no longer believe a photograph isn’t a AI fake (Case in point, a new species of Amazonian giant water lily was found from a social media post of a man swimming amongst the giant leaves. If the photo could be fake, why spend thousands of dollars trying to track down that rare plant deep in the jungle?) Similarly, in the future people will come to doubt the validity of past archival photographs, and REAL extinct species, from dodos to Carolina parakeets, will become, at least in the popular imagination, of the same fanciful ilk as unicorns and Bigfoot. We are corrupting reality itself with this AI slop.

One by one they dropped the relationship after decades. I didn't think I'd be one of them, and tried to preserve the relationship by setting firm boundaries. But ultimately even that failed, and in mid-1990s, when my daughter graduated from college and flat out refused to have this woman at our party, some thing changed. I initially insisted - good manners - but the softest-spoken woman in our group let me know in no uncertain terms, this was my daughter's day and her request should be respected. She was right, and that was the end. My friend withdrew for a long time, then eventually reached out. By that time I realized how exhausting it was to have a mentally ill person, highly reactive, high-wired person in my life, and I no longer respond. Wish her well, but I can never go back. If she had any other urgent situation in her life, I waited until after she had spoken with her caseworker and it had been at least 24 hours. Just because you love somebody doesn't mean that you are equipped or are the appropriate person to deal with their emergencies. I had that conversation with her when she was doing well. The statement that cued me is "severe and escalating".  That suggests that, in fact, the friend is not able to control her symptoms or manage the manic phases in a better way.  I would say the better way to approach "all that" is to level-set by speaking to her and her family (excluding maybe her child!) when she's able to hear you and speak to your concerns about her needs and her battle.  Not shaming her, but certainly NOT allowing her to triangulate or separate you from her other care circle members.  

Having lived with loving parents who both suffered from different forms of mental illness, I can tell you that it was as disruptive to me and those relationships.  It never was helpful to have an adult friend only listen to (a) parent-it augmented their leverage to continue with their maladaptive family patterns.  So refocus on the larger group who're being held hostage by this undertreated disease! 

This approach helps you, too: it firmly telegraphs that you are a caring person who looks at the needs of the family, not simply the dramas of the sufferer.  

If you can, and are allowed by both parents, please also consider spending time with the child-obviously as long as the child knows you and is comfortable with you-or if you're not that person, please support the child in having some other stable and loving adults in their life.  Speaking for the long-ago child, I wish that had been the case for me.

I find it helpful to think of the illness as the Other, an enemy whose invasion of my friend’s mind is preventing them from being themselves. I have my own Other, and it feels like an invasion when it happens to me. 

A dear friend goes through cycles of delusion and paranoia. He’ll cut all contact with me, except for the occasional angry text telling me to stop spying on his computer. (Is it necessary to state that I’m not?) We’ve had some terrible, agonizing arguments—and by “we” I mean his Other and I—which left me with the choice between walking away from someone I adore, or accepting that the pleasure of his company comes with the cost of suffering his bipolar downturns. If I didn’t love him so much, I don’t know that I could tolerate it. We’ve been through four or five of these episodes, and every time he starts to emerge from the delusions, popping up on my phone to say something besides “Stop spying on me,” I’m thrilled. It’s worth it, for me in particular, for this specific relationship. I hope LW can weigh the costs & benefits, decide accordingly, and feel confident in that decision.

comments.name: Gowan McAvity
comments.body: Withdrawal is hiding, which sometimes is called for to preserve the self, though ghosting creates guilt and personal quandaries, so if it’s an old friend and you’ve been through this before, know the score, and see the signs of mania, and excess, then a standard recognized response is called for, individualized for effect, to staunch the mania, that doesn’t engage the episode details, it engages the mania, such as, from my personal male perspective, “Dude, have you had a few? This sounds familiar, are you off your meds? What’s the doctor say?” This often turns the temperature down and the boundary is reestablished. I’ll listen, but I’m not traveling that road again. Then the whole thing is forgotten by the next conversation. It’s very difficult to do this with consistency and not be sucked in. In any event it is prudent to consistently suggest professional aid for the mania friend. If they don’t flee and look for other mania prey then they appreciate you and the boundaries set. High boundaries are called for in life sometimes to remain sane yourself.

comments.name: Nancy
comments.body:
LW doesn’t need a therapist. She needs to learn not to inhabit her friend’s fantasy world with her. That behavior helps neither one of them. If that means she cannot continue the friendship, that is the price. 

But perhaps some thought on how she comes to be gullible might help. Perhaps she enjoys being a savior. Is there a way to be friends in a less wrought manner?

comments.name: Michael you
comments.body:
The letter writer asks how to deal with someone whose mental illness leads her to cross the writer’s boundaries, but it’s hard to see what boundaries the writer has actually set. In the past, it appears they have been willing to jump feet first into emergencies even while knowing their friend’s propensity for imagining things. The writer mentions the woman has a spouse and close family, but doesn’t mention ever having talked to the spouse or other family members to verify what is going on and determine the best strategy to help. (Understood a pregnancy may not be something the writer could talk to the husband about, but other emergencies surely needed a broader consultation.) 

The issue, it seems to me, is not ethical but practical. The writer needs to learn to set true boundaries and resist the temptation to let their life be consumed by their friend’s problems, whether real or imaginary. They also need to consult with other others in the friend’s close circle to see how to respond when crises erupt. By managing their own response in future, they should be able to resume the friendship, which appears to be this writer’s ultimate (and worthy) goal.

comments.name: Dave
comments.body: Great article.  It is nice to see the founders of our modern understanding break into the NYT.  I only have one quibble, which is that Johannes Kepler and Tycho Brahe are missing from the discussion.  I would argue that Tycho at least co-owns with Galileo the honor as ‘founder of observational astronomy.’  His detailed and meticulous observations allowed Kepler to formulate his famous Laws of Planetary Motion, which refined the planet’s circular revolutions into more properly described elliptical orbits.

comments.name: Duttins
comments.body: Oh, my, as a former physics teacher, this overwhelms me. I have taught this science history but, never imagined that there were original copies extant. It is the precursor to modern physics when the next geniuses came along.

comments.name: John
comments.body:
A couple more things: First, it is now known, at least to historians of Islamic astronomy, that the mathematics of Copernicus' book was derived from 14th century Arab models, probably through inspection of the diagrams in an Arabic manuscript, which would have been understandable to a competent astronomer, which Copernicus certainly was. Islamic astronomers had not made the leap to heliocentrism, but they seem to have laid the grounds for it. Second, it was not until later astronomers, notably Kepler and Tycho, that the heliocentric system could comfortably predict celestial motions. Some of the giants whose shoulders Newton stood upon were Muslim.
Nonetheless, I would happily trade my first-born son for any one of these books. One of the deep spiritual experiences of my life was holding in my hands an original copy of the first edition of Kant's "Critique of Pure Reason."

Two corrections, according to my knowledge.  Newton's book is generally known as "the Principia", at least in my circles.  Also, Newton did not discover gravity; he discovered universal gravity: a dramatic development that ended the special place of the heavens.  More than that, Newton's book changed the nature of science, and that was recognized at the time.  I'm awed by just thinking about it.

comments.body:
As someone who sold Calvin Klein Collection at retail in the late 90s and early 2000s when it was riding high before his retirement, it is endlessly disappointing to see replacement designers who can't see past the 1990s in their inspiration, and get mired in boxy black and grey silhouettes. Calvin's customers loved his clothes because he made great American designer sportswear that they could trust and rely on. Women would walk into the store and say, "I need a new black suit" with full confidence that it would be the perfect black suit for that moment in time. And it was.
And then also there was a runway collection  which, truth be told, could occasionally miss. A look at Calvin's rich archives, however, back through the 70s and 80s would find color, exuberance and lots of sexy clothes without obvious vulgarity. I ca't tell you how many great jersey dresses are in there that anyone would jump at today. Raf Simons was a gutsy move that looked great on paper, and I agree that he did what he was hired to do, but the sales that skyrocketed in anticipation and then plummeted when customers roundly rejected the clothes showed that the label really does have a strong concept and image that he simply didn't understand or chose to ignore. 
I still have a lot of affection for the Collection label and admiration for what Calvin accomplished, and I still hold out hope for someone to come in who has an expansive understanding of the brand beyond jeans and sexy perfume ads.
